mechanism: An agent argues what MUST be true ("only happens if git-connected", "so CLI-only holds") instead of quoting a value it actually read.
consequence: A plausible inference gets recorded as verified runtime truth; downstream readers treat it as checked.
instance: Three argued-not-read claims landed in one session; two reached the project's correction ledger before being caught.
fix: A linter flags any ledger row whose evidence field argues a mechanism with no cited read value (flag, not block). 0/87 false positives on the live ledger at the time it shipped.

mechanism: Same pattern: an agent inferred an LLM call existed in a pipeline from its shape, without reading the code.
consequence: A fleet-classification report named an LLM lane that no `claude` invocation actually backed.
instance: Caught the same day the report was written, during a routine code read.
fix: Same linter guard as above; not yet extended to catch this reasoning pattern inside prose reports (only ledger rows).

mechanism: A containment check enumerates the cases it already knows about and reports the result as the total.
consequence: "0 tracked" reads as exhaustive when it only covered the paths the check's author remembered to list.
instance: A cleanup verified five known root config-cache paths were untracked by git; 22 nested capture files were still tracked in two repos the check never walked.
fix: Recursive, pattern-based scans replace fixed path lists for any "is X fully removed" claim.

mechanism: A secret-pattern scan matched a committed blob but not the full history of renamed/moved copies of the same file.
consequence: "0 credential shapes in any committed blob" was reported while one token sat in 16 historical blobs the scan's scope never reached.
instance: Found by widening the scan to full history rather than trusting the first bounded pass.
fix: Any "0 found" claim now states what was scanned (working tree vs. full history vs. one repo) alongside the count.

mechanism: A consumption audit keyed its file scan on a dated-filename pattern.
consequence: One real, actively-read status document never matched the pattern and was silently excluded from the audit's "who reads this" answer.
instance: Found when the audited document's own update cadence didn't match the audit's conclusion about it.
fix: Filename-pattern scans are treated as a floor, not a ceiling, on "everything" claims; a second pass checks known high-traffic files by name.

mechanism: A capability's live/dead state changes, but nothing pushes that change to the status surfaces that cached the old state.
consequence: A status line claimed a phone-push integration was "armed, live in production" for ten days while every scheduled run logged the integration variable as unset and the push as skipped.
instance: Surfaced by reading the run log directly instead of trusting the status line.
fix: Status lines for toggleable integrations are now derived from the same run log that would log the skip, not hand-set at the moment of wiring.

mechanism: A kill verdict on a scheduled job was recorded against an old build of that job.
consequence: The job stayed "killed" in the record for a window where the fixed version had actually run zero times — the verdict and the evidence had diverged.
instance: Caught when the verdict's timestamp was checked against the job's own fix-commit timestamp.
fix: A kill/pin verdict now carries the commit hash of the code it was measured against, not just a verdict string.

mechanism: A CLI auth token for a hosting provider expires on a short (~8h) cycle; the integration reading it does not check expiry before use.
consequence: A dashboard panel reading "what's live" degrades to silently empty between CLI re-logins, with no error surfaced.
instance: Found while auditing why a live-status panel intermittently showed nothing.
fix: Not yet guarded — logged as an open gap pending a token-freshness check before the panel renders.

mechanism: An OAuth grant for a background integration can be revoked server-side; the client only discovers this on its next call, as a generic error.
consequence: A silent `invalid_grant` failure looks identical to a transient network error unless something explicitly checks for it.
instance: A dedicated healthcheck probe was added specifically because this class of revocation produces no proactive signal.
fix: A recurring probe calls the integration specifically to surface `invalid_grant` as a distinct, actionable alert.

mechanism: A monitoring sweep's own prior-run marker ("seen") was read back by the same sweep as if it were new incoming data.
consequence: A live decision tap was reported as an ignored/dropped event, when it was the sweep's own earlier pass that had already marked it seen.
instance: Found by tracing the specific event ID back to the process that had set the "seen" flag.
fix: A sweep now excludes records it itself produced from its own "were any events dropped" count.

mechanism: A status-classifying regex matched a negated phrase ("un-retired") as if it were the positive claim ("retired").
consequence: An active workstream was reported as sentenced/retired based on a false-positive string match.
instance: Caught when the workstream's actual recent activity contradicted its reported retirement.
fix: Negation-aware matching plus a proximity window around the matched keyword, re-verified against a fixed set of known false-positive strings.

mechanism: A second, unrelated use of the same keyword appeared ~500 characters later in the same document and won the classification.
consequence: A data-collection lane was judged "retired" on a keyword hit that belonged to a different paragraph's unrelated topic.
instance: Fixed the same audit pass as the row above, same underlying regex weakness.
fix: A tighter proximity window plus exclusion of the ledger document itself from verdict scans (a document that CATALOGS retirements is not evidence a given lane was retired).

mechanism: A background-task watchdog kills a long-running job once free system memory drops below roughly 1.5 GB of 16 GB total, and reports the kill with wording indistinguishable from a real OS out-of-memory kill.
consequence: Four kills in one session were all diagnosed as "the machine ran out of memory from other apps"; the actual fix (don't run heavy jobs as foreground/attached tasks) was never tried because the wrong cause was assumed.
instance: An index-build job died 40 minutes in; a second index build plus a concurrent benchmark died together 20 minutes later; a third, later, died loading a ~5.3 GB model (that one genuinely was a fit problem, which reinforced the wrong diagnosis).
fix: Any long-running index/benchmark/model-load job launches fully DETACHED from the controlling tool (its own OS process, hidden window, output redirected to a log, PID captured) — the watchdog only supervises jobs it tracks as its own.

mechanism: A process-liveness check matched running processes by a command-line substring, and the scanning shell's own command line (and its wrapper shells) contained that same substring.
consequence: A kill selector built from the same substring match killed the very shells running the diagnostic, logged as unrelated process failures.
instance: A `*vault_search.py --index*` command-line match killed the session's own wrapper shells mid-diagnosis.
fix: Liveness/kill selectors must match on process name AND path, or on a PID captured at the job's own launch — never on a substring the scanning command itself also contains; interactive shells are excluded from any "is X still running" count.

mechanism: The same watchdog killed a job mid-model-load with 2.35 GB free and nothing else competing for memory running alongside it.
consequence: This was the row that finally falsified the "it's always near 1.5 GB free, caused by other apps" theory — a wider margin, same kill, no other apps running.
instance: The identical command, re-launched fully detached seven minutes later (PID captured, hidden window, output to a log), ran 73 minutes to completion untouched.
fix: Detached-launch is the only confirmed guard; the watchdog's real threshold is still not fully characterized.

mechanism: A later measurement of the same watchdog found it killing a job with 4.1 GB of 15.83 GB free — well above the ~1.5 GB figure from the prior incident.
consequence: The ~1.5 GB number had been treated as a threshold rather than one observation; it wasn't predictive on its own.
instance: A recursive search over a large dependency tree was killed at 4.1 GB free, measured at the moment of the kill.
fix: Treat any single observed threshold as a lower bound on risk, not a safe-zone cutoff; the detached-launch guard (not a memory margin) is what actually held in every later case.

mechanism: A looping background process treats a missing required credential or endpoint as a startup warning and then keeps looping instead of exiting.
consequence: Every cycle fails at the exact same point, silently, while every liveness signal (heartbeat, process alive, scheduler state) stays green — nothing distinguishes "idle because there's no work" from "idle because it's broken".
instance: A sync daemon restarted after a boot, found a renamed config key missing, logged one warning, then ran 568 five-minute cycles each failing on the same missing value — about 48 hours before anything caught it.
fix: A daemon whose required input is unavailable now exits non-zero immediately instead of warning and continuing; a separate monitor watches OUTPUT age (not just heartbeat/process-alive) with a 48-hour threshold.

mechanism: Same shape as above: a notification integration treats a missing topic/endpoint config as "skip this push" rather than a startup failure.
consequence: A status line said a phone-push alert was armed and live for ten days while every run logged the push as skipped for lack of a configured topic.
instance: Also the founding instance of the revocation-doesn't-propagate row dated 2026-09-03 above — one root cause, two consequences.
fix: Same fix pattern: fail loud on a missing required input, don't warn-and-continue.

mechanism: A test asserts an invariant against a fixture it constructs itself (a seeded fresh dataset, a hand-written dict) rather than against the artifact the program actually writes to disk.
consequence: A green self-check sat on top of a genuinely broken shipped artifact — worse than no check, because the green reads as evidence the shipped file is sound and nothing else is watching it.
instance: A life-simulation script seeded a fresh world and asserted a relationship invariant held — and passed — while the shipped output file showed two entities each committed to a third party who was committed to neither.
fix: A self-check for any script that SHIPS a file must assert its invariant against that file after the normal write path, not only against a constructed fixture.

mechanism: The underlying state was repaired, but a historical per-step snapshot used for replay/export was generated before the fix and never regenerated.
consequence: Re-running the exporter after the fix could never clear the bug, because "current state is correct" and "the history I export from is correct" are two separate claims, and the fix only shipped the first one.
instance: Same session as the row above, discovered immediately after the first fix landed.
fix: Any fix to current state is checked against exported/replayed history separately — fixing the source does not retroactively fix prior artifacts derived from the old, broken state.

mechanism: A repo-wide audit of self-checks (parsed ~300 files) found the large majority asserted only against constructed fixtures, with a traceable downstream consumer of the real output in most of those cases.
consequence: A codebase can carry hundreds of green checks while most of the actual shipped outputs they're meant to protect are unchecked.
instance: Of 165 scripts with a self-check, the audit found roughly 80% fixture-only, a small minority exercising both, and none doing a pure smoke test of the real output end to end.
fix: No blanket fix shipped; the audit is treated as a standing backlog, prioritized by which fixture-only checks guard the highest-blast-radius outputs.

mechanism: A session-lifecycle hook (added for an interactive-use feature) runs unconditionally, including when the same CLI is invoked headlessly from a scheduler.
consequence: Every scheduled, unattended invocation of the CLI started exiting with a non-zero status for a reason unrelated to the task it was supposed to run — the hook, not the task, was failing.
instance: Six separate scheduled call sites broke the same day the hook was added; the fix was a one-line settings flag disabling all hooks on each headless call site.
fix: Headless/scheduled invocations of the CLI now explicitly disable session hooks at the call site instead of assuming the interactive default is safe everywhere.

mechanism: A probe agent's own cleanup step killed a browser process by NAME (a process-kill command that matches every process sharing that executable name) instead of by the specific process ID it had launched.
consequence: The cleanup command matched and force-closed the operator's own, unrelated, in-use browser session running on the same machine — not just the probe's throwaway instance.
instance: Open tabs were recoverable from a session snapshot written minutes earlier; anything unsaved in an open form or composer at that moment was not recoverable.
fix: Any cleanup step kills by the specific PID (or handle) captured at launch time — never by process name, and never by a selector broad enough to match something the operator, not the agent, owns.
